question: Why are spring tides higher than neap tides?
expected: At spring tides the Sun, Earth and Moon are lined up, so the Sun's and the Moon's pulls add; at neap tides the Moon is at a right angle to the Sun and the pulls partly cancel.
passage: Tides are raised mostly by the Moon. Its gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it than on the far side, and that difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, one toward the Moon and one away from it. As the Earth turns under the bulges, most coasts see two high tides and two low tides in a little under 25 hours. The Sun raises tides as well, though only about half as strong, because it is so much farther away. When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the two pulls add and the tides run high; these are spring tides. When the Moon is at a right angle to the Sun, at the quarter moons, the pulls partly cancel and the range is small; these are neap tides.
answer: When the sun and moon are in a line with the earth their gravity works together so the tides get bigger. At neap they're at 90 degrees and work against each other.
label: right

question: Why does a question asked a few days after reading help memory more than the same question asked a minute after?
expected: Recall strengthens a memory most when some forgetting has happened first, so the answer comes back with effort; a minute after reading it comes back too easily to do much.
passage: Rereading a chapter feels productive because the text becomes familiar, and familiarity is easy to mistake for knowing. Testing yourself works differently. Each time you pull an idea out of memory without looking, the memory becomes easier to reach the next time, and the effort of reaching is part of what strengthens it. This is why a recall attempt that fails, followed by checking the answer, still helps more than reading the answer twice. The benefit is largest when some forgetting has happened first: a question answered a minute after reading does little, while the same question a few days later, when the answer comes back with difficulty, does much more.
answer: After a few days you've partly forgotten it, so you have to work to get it back, and that effort is what makes the memory stronger. A minute later it's still sitting there so there's no effort.
label: right

question: How does a write-ahead log let a database recover from a crash without ending up half-changed?
expected: Every change is recorded in the log and forced to disk before the data page is written, so after a crash the database replays the logged changes of committed transactions and undoes those of uncommitted ones.
passage: A database that crashes halfway through a change must not come back half-changed. The usual protection is a write-ahead log. Before the database alters any page of its data files, it appends a record describing the change to the log and forces that record to disk. Only then may the data page itself be written, and that can happen lazily, seconds or minutes later. After a crash, the database reads the log from the last checkpoint forward, replays every record whose transaction committed, and undoes the changes of transactions that did not. Appending to a log is fast because the writes are sequential, which is why committing a transaction costs one small log write and not a scattered rewrite of every page it touched.
answer: Changes go into the log first, on disk, before the real data is touched. On restart it goes through the log, redoes anything that was committed and rolls back whatever wasn't.
label: right

question: Why did the Harrow Canal lose its traffic after 1843?
expected: The Astley and Dunmere Railway opened along almost the same route and cut the journey from about nine hours to under an hour.
passage: The Harrow Canal opened in 1811 to carry coal from the Dunmere pits to the mills at Astley, a distance of fourteen miles. It climbed 96 feet through twelve locks, and a loaded barge took about nine hours to make the trip. For three decades it paid its shareholders well. Then in 1843 the Astley and Dunmere Railway opened along almost the same route and cut the journey to under an hour. The canal company halved its tolls within a year, but traffic kept falling, and in 1858 it sold the canal to the railway, which kept it open only as a water supply for its engines.
answer: A railway opened on nearly the same route and it was far faster, under an hour instead of nine.

question: Why does compost improve both clay soil and sandy soil?
expected: In clay it binds the particles into crumbs with wider gaps between them, so water drains; in sand it acts as a sponge that holds water the grains would let go.
passage: Clay soils hold water because their particles are tiny and flat, which leaves only very narrow gaps between them. Water clings to the walls of narrow gaps and drains slowly, so a clay soil stays wet long after rain. Sandy soils are the opposite: their grains are large, the gaps between them are wide, and water runs straight through. That is why a sandy bed needs watering often while a clay bed can drown roots that sit in it. Adding compost helps both. In clay it binds particles into crumbs with wider gaps between them, so water drains; in sand it acts as a sponge that holds water the grains would let go.
answer: In clay it clumps the tiny particles together so there are bigger spaces and the water can get out. In sand it soaks up water like a sponge so it doesn't all run through.
label: right

question: Why do most coasts see two high tides a day rather than one?
expected: The Moon's pull stretches the oceans into two bulges, one toward the Moon and one away from it, and the Earth turns under both of them in a little under 25 hours.
passage: Tides are raised mostly by the Moon. Its gravity pulls harder on the side of the Earth facing it than on the far side, and that difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, one toward the Moon and one away from it. As the Earth turns under the bulges, most coasts see two high tides and two low tides in a little under 25 hours. The Sun raises tides as well, though only about half as strong, because it is so much farther away. When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the two pulls add and the tides run high; these are spring tides. When the Moon is at a right angle to the Sun, at the quarter moons, the pulls partly cancel and the range is small; these are neap tides.
answer: There are two bulges of water, one on the side facing the moon and one on the opposite side, and the earth's rotation carries a coast through both of them each day.
